## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Industrial production of antibiotics
### alcoholic beverages
### citric acid

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The same fermentation principle, scaled to tonnes: a **fermenter** (bioreactor) grows the microbe under controlled temperature, pH and aeration, and the product is harvested, purified and marketed. The three NEB exemplars: **penicillin** (the first antibiotic, discovered by Fleming in 1928, mass-produced in WWII), **ethanol** for beverages (*Saccharomyces*), and **citric acid** (*Aspergillus niger*).

**Concept flow — from lab discovery to industrial fermenter (study in this order)**

| Step | Stage | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Discovery | Fleming notices Penicillium killing staphylococci (1928); Florey and Chain purify it (1940s) |
| 2 | Strain selection and improvement | Highest-yielding strain chosen; mutated for more product |
| 3 | Medium preparation | Sterilised nutrient broth (sugar, nitrogen, minerals) loaded into the fermenter |
| 4 | Inoculation and growth | Pure culture added; temperature, pH, oxygen controlled by probes |
| 5 | Production phase | Microbe secretes the product into the broth (or into cells) |
| 6 | Downstream processing | Filtration, extraction, purification, drying, quality control, packaging |

**Industrial products — microbe, substrate and product**

| Product | Microbe | Substrate / process | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Penicillin | Penicillium notatum / chrysogenum (fungus) | Aerobic fermentation on corn-steep liquor medium | Antibiotic against Gram-positive bacteria |
| Ethanol (beer, wine) | Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) | Barley malt (beer) or grape juice (wine), anaerobic fermentation | Alcoholic beverages; industrial ethanol |
| Citric acid | Aspergillus niger (fungus) | Aerobic fermentation on molasses/sugar | Food preservative, flavouring, soft drinks |
| Note — antibiotics kill other microbes | Selected strains yield the most drug per litre | Fermenter keeps conditions at the optimum | Downstream purification is half the cost |

**Inside the fermenter — the parts and their jobs**

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| Stirrer (impeller) | Mixes the broth evenly; keeps microbes suspended |
| Sparger / aeration system | Delivers sterile air or oxygen for aerobic fermentations |
| Temperature and pH probes | Keep conditions at the optimum for the strain |
| Sterile inlet / inoculum port | Lets the pure culture in without contamination |
| Harvest outlet / product drain | Removes broth for downstream processing |
| Cooling jacket | Carries away metabolic heat — fermentation is exothermic |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — penicillin's scale-up.** Fleming's plate gave a halo of killed bacteria around a *Penicillium* colony, but the yield was tiny. Industrial production needed: (1) a higher-yielding strain (from *P. notatum* to *P. chrysogenum*, then X-ray-mutated strains), (2) a better medium (corn-steep liquor), (3) aerated stirred fermenters, because the mould is aerobic, and (4) downstream extraction. Lesson: a discovery becomes a drug only when the fermenter economics work — strain, medium and engineering all three.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Antibiotic: Penicillium notatum/chrysogenum → penicillin (Fleming 1928, Chain & Florey purified); 'antibiotic' = against life — the discovery story earns the mark.
Trick 2: Alcohol: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (brewer's yeast) ferments malted grains/fruit juice; distilled spirits vs beer/wine — the yeast is the same in all.
Trick 3: Citric acid: Aspergillus niger; also acetic acid (Acetobacter), lactic acid (Lactobacillus) — the industrial chemicals table.
Trick 4: Fermenters provide: sterile medium, aeration, temperature control, pH — the four conditions for industrial scale-up.
